description:
Every command arm that accepts the machine-readable output flag reports its failures in the structured error envelope, so a machine consumer never has to parse a plain-text diagnostic line.

## Background

The machine-readable contract covers success output but not failure. An arm that renders the envelope on failure does so by classifying the error at its own call site; nine distinct mechanisms do this today, including a shared macro at `crates/jit/src/output_macros.rs:70`, five named helper functions, and 35 inline sites that print an envelope and exit directly. An arm that instead propagates its error with a bare `?` reaches the top-level printer, which writes a plain-text `Error: <message>` line to stderr and leaves stdout empty. The plain-text form carries no error code, no structured detail, and nothing a JSON parser can read.

Measured on the current tree: 99 command arms accept the flag. 51 of them have no envelope route on any failure path, and several of the remaining 48 classify only one error class and propagate the rest. Confirmed by invocation against a missing or invalid argument — `issue show`, `gate status`, `item show`, and `dep add` emit the envelope, while `doc list`, `doc show`, and `graph deps` leave stdout empty and write the plain line to stderr. So the defect is neither universal nor confined to one namespace, and which arms are affected is not derivable from the command surface itself.

Exit codes diverge as well. Nine arms exit differently under the flag than without it, because the code string their envelope carries is absent from the registered error-code vocabulary and falls through to the generic class: `dep add` exits 3 plain and 1 under the flag, `gate define` exits 6 plain and 1 under the flag, and `gate preset apply` exits 1 plain and 0 under the flag, folding its per-issue failures into a success payload. The generated exit-code reference documents the plain-path values, and its binding test exercises only the plain path, so the projection is accurate for one invocation form and silently wrong for the other.

The `doc` namespace is where it surfaced: nine arms there (`add`, `list`, `remove`, `show`, `history`, `diff`, `assets list`, `check-links`, `conformance`) propagate with a bare `?`, and `doc dir` was repaired in place, establishing one of the nine patterns — classify the failure by downcast, then hand the envelope to the shared macro.

This surface is what the MCP bridge is generated from. An agent consumer reaching a failing arm receives `EXECUTION_ERROR` with the plain-text diagnostic embedded in a shell-command string, so the failure reason is undecodable without parsing prose.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A census derived from the command definitions, rather than from sampling, records for every arm accepting the machine-readable output flag whether its failure path renders the structured envelope.
- [hard] REQ-02: Every arm accepting the flag renders its failures as the structured error envelope carrying a classified error code, with no arm reaching the top-level plain-text printer.
- [hard] REQ-03: A failing invocation under the flag emits no plain-text diagnostic on the stream that carries the envelope.
- [hard] REQ-04: A converted arm's process exit code equals the code its envelope reports, and failures of the same class exit identically across arms.
- [hard] REQ-05: Regression coverage drives a failing invocation of every converted arm and asserts envelope structure and error classification rather than a copied message string.
- [hard] REQ-06: A repository check fails when an arm accepting the flag can reach the top-level plain-text printer on failure, so a newly added arm cannot ship without the envelope.
- [hard] REQ-07: Adopter documentation states the machine-readable failure contract — envelope shape, error code, exit code — once, in a single canonical home.

## Non-goals

- Changing the human-readable failure output of any command.
- Restructuring the success-side envelope or its collection wrapper.
- Renaming or removing any error code a command already emits.
- Adding the flag to command arms that do not accept it today.

## Notes

- Scope is the whole command surface rather than the `doc` namespace alone, and delivery is in milestone v1.0: the plain-text failure form is a release-visible contract defect on the surface generated agent tooling consumes, and a repair pattern is already established in the tree.
- REQ-04 requires the exit code to follow the reported code, so the nine measured divergences move. The code strings themselves stay, which is why the non-goal above forbids renaming rather than forbidding all vocabulary change.
- REQ-07 is subject to `@/charter/D-13`: one canonical home per adopter-facing fact.
- REQ-06 is what separates this from a sweep. The census in REQ-01 goes stale the moment a new arm is added, so the guard is the durable half of the work.
title: Structured failure reporting across the machine-readable CLI surface
